sections.h2: What should you know before selling a house in Brownsville, TX?
sections.html:
Brownsville is the county seat of Cameron County, at the southernmost tip of Texas across the Rio Grande from Matamoros. Sellers deal with the Cameron Appraisal District, the county clerk and a border economy built on trade and a deepwater port.

The Census Bureau puts the mid-2025 population at 192,957, which is 3.6% above the 2020 estimates base. Residents often handle paperwork in two languages, since 83.6% of people age five and older speak another language at home.

sections.h2: How did the border, the river and the port shape Brownsville neighborhoods?
sections.html:
Per the Handbook of Texas, the town started beside Fort Brown, named for an officer killed during the 1846 siege. Charles Stillman and partners platted a 4,676 acre townsite in 1848, lots sold for as much as $1,500, and the new Cameron County seat was Brownsville by January 13, 1849.

Ownership of the original land grant stayed contested until a U.S. Supreme Court decision in 1879. The first train arrived in 1904, a rail bridge to Matamoros opened in 1910, and northern farmers introduced irrigated citrus and vegetables. A 1920s land boom lifted the population to 22,021 by 1930. Voters approved a navigation district in December 1928, and the port opened May 15, 1936, using a 17-mile channel to the Gulf.

After the war, shrimpers from Texas and Louisiana made the town a leading shrimp shipper, and cotton briefly turned the port into the world's top cotton exporter in the early 1950s. A Union Carbide plant started construction in 1959. Each of those booms added housing and jobs to the city.

  • Southern end of U.S. highways 77 and 83
  • Postwar shrimp, citrus and cotton shipping, then petrochemicals
  • The fort was deactivated in 1945 and its grounds were eventually given to the city
  • Palmito Ranch, the last Civil War battle, was fought just outside town in 1865

sections.h2: What do Census figures say about Brownsville homes?
sections.html:
The 2020-2024 midpoint for an owner-occupied Brownsville home is $139,900, and 61.7% of units are lived in by owners. Renters pay a midpoint of $923 a month.

The city covers 131.53 square miles of land, and 27.5% of residents were born abroad. A drive to work averages 21.4 minutes.

sections.h2: Who sets the value of a Brownsville house for tax purposes?
sections.html:
The Cameron Appraisal District sets value, and each taxing unit chooses its own rate. By its own FAQ, the district reappraises every property at least once in three years and can do so yearly where the market moves fast.

A notice of appraised value is not required if value rises by $1,000 or less, so some owners never get a mailing. A homestead's assessed value is capped at 10% growth under Section 23.23 of the Tax Code, in force since January 1, 2008. Added rooms, pools and similar improvements are not covered.

sections.h2: How do homestead exemptions work with the Cameron Appraisal District?
sections.html:
Every owner must show Texas residency, such as a driver's license, and both spouses must apply and supply identification. The primary residence exemptions are homestead, over-65, disabled person and 100% disabled veteran, while a disabled veteran exemption may be placed on any one property the veteran owns.

  • You may claim over-65 or disabled in a year, not both
  • When only some co-owners live in the house, the account splits and the exemption is multiplied by the qualifying owner's percentage of ownership
  • The school tax ceiling rises if you add a pool, garage or room, and transfers to a new Texas homestead on a Tax Ceiling Transfer form

A few exemption types need a fresh application by April 30 every year, so ask the district which applies.

sections.h2: How do you contest a Brownsville appraisal?
sections.html:
The protest has to be written, and the deadline is the later of May 15 or 30 days after the notice was delivered. Mail, hand delivery and email all work, with mailed filings needing a postmark by the cutoff.

The district states that after the deadline neither an appraiser nor the board may change the value. Hospitalization can be good cause, but forgetting the date is not. A timely protest earns at least 15 days' notice of a hearing that usually runs about 15 minutes. Disputing the result opens three options: district court, binding arbitration, or, in Cameron County, the State Office of Administrative Hearings.

  • Identify the owner and the property by address or account number
  • Say what you contest, such as market value
  • Attach comparable sales, photos or repair estimates

sections.h2: How does the Texas tax calendar affect a Brownsville seller?
sections.html:
Value and lien both date to January 1. The Cameron County Tax Office sits at the same East Levee Street address as the clerk, and bills arrive around October 1. Ask that office which units bill your address.

Unpaid balances go delinquent February 1 and pick up a six percent penalty plus one percent interest. The penalty becomes 12 percent after July 1, and a taxing unit's attorney may add as much as 20 percent. Clear title is impossible with delinquent tax outstanding, so pay any balance before closing.

sections.h2: What if a Brownsville property is headed for a tax sale?
sections.html:
Constables or hired agents run tax sales as auctions, and no statewide list exists. County tax office and clerk sites carry the notices.

A homestead, farm or mineral owner can redeem within two years of the purchaser's deed being filed, paying a 25% premium in year one or 50% in year two plus costs. Other property has 180 days and a premium up to 25%. A former owner has two years from the sale to claim surplus proceeds.

sections.h2: How do heirs handle an inherited Brownsville house?
sections.html:
Family land in the Valley sometimes stays in the name of a person who died long ago. An affidavit of heirship is sworn and filed with the county clerk, but no court reviews it and nothing requires a title insurer to accept it.

Sturdier paths include probate inside four years, a muniment of title where the only debts are liens on the real estate, or a transfer on death deed filed before the owner's death. For exemption purposes, heirs missing from a recorded deed give the appraisal district an affidavit of ownership interest, the death certificate and a recent utility bill.

sections.h2: Where does a Brownsville deed get recorded?
sections.html:
The Cameron County Clerk, at 835 E. Levee Street in Brownsville, keeps deeds, liens, plats and maps. Cameron CAD updates ownership after it receives a recorded instrument or its volume and page numbers.

The state clerk manual lists a $5.00 first page and $4.00 for each added page, with further fees. Ask the clerk for the total on your deed.

faqs.q: What does a typical Brownsville home cost?
faqs.a: The Census Bureau's 2020-2024 midpoint for owner-occupied homes is $139,900. Your own price depends on condition, lot and street.

faqs.q: Will Cameron CAD always mail a value notice?
faqs.a: No. It sends notices to those entitled by law, and none is required when value rises by $1,000 or less.

faqs.q: When is a Brownsville appraisal protest due?
faqs.a: The later of May 15 or 30 days after the notice was delivered. File it in writing by mail, by hand or by email.

faqs.q: Where can I get a copy of my Brownsville deed?
faqs.a: At the Cameron County Clerk's office on East Levee Street. The appraisal district does not supply deeds, surveys or plats.

faqs.q: Does a Brownsville homeowner over 65 get a tax ceiling?
faqs.a: Yes. School taxes on the residence generally stop rising while you own and live there, and the ceiling can move to a new Texas homestead.
